title: You’ve said it before. Maybe quietly. Maybe out loud when no one was watching.
paragraphs: You’ve said it before. Maybe quietly. Maybe out loud when no one was watching.
“I’m just following my heart.”
It sounded honest. It felt right. It even gave you peace for a moment.
But then came the consequences you didn’t expect.
Because the same heart you trusted… is the one that led you there.

The late-night decision you knew you shouldn’t make.
The relationship you forced even when the warning signs were loud.
The compromise you justified because it “felt right.”

God saw it.
You knew.
But here’s what most people don’t realize…
The most dangerous advice you’ve ever been given isn’t “hate people,” or “do evil.”

It’s softer than that.
It sounds harmless.
It even sounds spiritual.
“Follow your heart.”
And Scripture doesn’t just disagree with that idea.
It exposes it.
“The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it?” — Jeremiah 17:9
Read that again.

Not slightly flawed.
Not occasionally mistaken.
Deceitful above all things.
That means your heart can lie to you better than anyone else can.

It can make sin feel justified.
It can dress rebellion as freedom.
It can make disobedience feel like destiny.
You’ve felt that, haven’t you?
That moment where everything inside you said “go,” but something deeper—quieter—was warning you to stop.
And you ignored it.
Because your heart was louder.
Originally written by Gospel Warrior.
The problem isn’t that you feel deeply. God created you with emotions.
The problem is that your heart was never meant to lead you.
It was corrupted.

When sin entered the world, it didn’t just affect behavior—it affected desire.
It twisted what you love.
It distorted what you crave.
That’s why Proverbs doesn’t say “follow your heart.”
It says, “Trust in the Lord with all your heart; and lean not unto your own understanding.” — Proverbs 3:5
Do you see the difference?

Not follow.
Trust God with it.
Your heart was meant to be surrendered, not obeyed.
Because left unchecked, it will always drift.

Toward pride.
Toward lust.
Toward self-glory.
You don’t have to train your heart to sin.
It already knows how.
That’s why Jesus said something that cuts deeper than most people are willing to admit:
“For from within, out of the heart of men, proceed evil thoughts, adulteries, fornications, murders…” — Mark 7:21
This isn’t about “being a good person.”
This is about recognizing that the problem is inside you.

Not your environment.
Not your past.
Not other people.
You.
And that’s where it gets uncomfortable.
Because if your heart can’t be trusted…
Then what can?
There was a moment—quiet, brutal, unavoidable—where everything had to be exposed.

Not just actions.
Not just habits.
But the core of who we are.
And this is where the Gospel steps in—not as a suggestion, but as a rescue.
“Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me.” — Psalm 51:10
That’s the cry of someone who finally understood:

My heart isn’t just wounded.
It’s broken beyond self-repair.
You can’t fix your heart by following it.
You need a new one.
And God promised exactly that.
“A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you…” — Ezekiel 36:26

Not improved.
Not upgraded.
New.
This is why Jesus didn’t come to guide your existing desires.
He came to crucify them… and give you life.
Because the cross wasn’t just about forgiveness.
It was about transformation.
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.” — 2 Corinthians 5:17
Two paths are in front of you right now, whether you admit it or not.

One where you keep trusting your heart…
…and slowly justify things you once knew were wrong.

And one where you surrender it…
…and let God reshape what you desire.

One leads to deception that feels like freedom.
The other leads to surrender that becomes real freedom.
You already know which one you’ve been choosing.

God saw it.
You knew.
But this isn’t the end of your story.
This is the moment where it can change.

Not by trying harder.
Not by “being better.”
But by turning.
Repenting.
Bringing your heart—the real one, not the filtered version—before God and admitting the truth:
“I can’t trust this.”
That’s where grace meets you.

Not when you defend your heart…
…but when you surrender it.
Say it.
“I need a new heart.”
Let that be real.
There’s more of this—deeper truth, sharper correction, real discipleship that doesn’t flatter your flesh but transforms your life.
Because silence is where deception survives.
Follow the journey. Stay close to truth.
